0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 31 December 1968, after the draft finalized by the Welding General Sectinnal Committee had been approved by the Structural and Metals Division Council. 0.2 The Sectional Committee responsible for the preparation of this standard felt the necessity for standardization of dimensional requirements for spot-welding electrodes in order to ensure the interchargeability of electrodes in the sockets of electrode holders and also to help in obtaining This standard lays down suitable cdde welds of uniform characteristics. numbers and dimensions for such electrodes so that the requirements for maximum number of applications are satisfied. However, these dimensions may be modified to suit the requirements for particular applications, if The requirements of the material recommended for these elecnecessary. trodes have also been included. 0.3 This standard has been prepared in two sections incorporating ` IS0 taper ' dimensions in one and ' Morse taper ' pimensions in the other for spotwelding electrodes. It has been decided that both&ese tapers may continue for the manufacture of spot-welding electrodes until such time the country changes over to IS0 taper. 0.4 This standard keeps in view the trade practices followed in the country in this field. Due regard has been taken of the Draft IS0 Recommendation on taper dimensions of electrodes and holders in the formulation of Section l of the standard which deals with spot-welding electrodes incorporating the taper dimensions as suggesred in the IS0 Rccomn:endation. It is felt that adoption of this taper will facilitate easy removal of electrodes from their Morse taper being followed in the country for the mL1nufacture of holders. spot-welding electrodes has been incorporated in Section 2 of this standard. 0.4.1 In the formulation of this standard? assistance ed from the following publications: has also been deriv-

ISO/R 670: 1968 Dimensions of straight resistance spot welding International Organization for Standardization. electrodes. 3

Draft IS0 Recommendation No. 1161 Dimensions of straight spot welding electrodes ( for loads greater than 1500 kgf). September 1966. Sizes 1 to 4 are for straight loading when the force does not exceed 1500 kgf. If the line of force comes outside the engaged diameter at the datum or gauge plane, then the loading should be deemed to be eccentric and the sizes 5 to 8 shall be used. If the force exceeds 1500 kgf for straight loading, then sizes 9 and 10 shall be used. 5. SHANKS 5.1 The shanks Table 1. of electrodes shall conform to the dimensions shown in I

6.2 If a non-circular hole is used, the area shall he not less than 30 percent nor more than 40 percent of shank area at the datum or gauge plane (engage diameter R) and dimensions of the hole shall be such that they admit a cooling pipe of appropriate outside diameter as follows: Nominal Size of Electrodes ( See Table 1) mm 1 and 5 2 and 6 3 and 7 4 and 8 9 10 Maximum Outside Diameter of Ccoling Pi@ mm 6 7 8 10 10 12

6.2.1 Cooling Pipe-The size of the cooling .pipe shall be such that the cross-sectional area of its bore is approximately equal to the area of the annulus formed between its outside diameter and the bore of the electrode. The cooling pipe shall he able to extend to within 4 mm from the blind end of the cooling hole in the electrode with the pipe and cut at 45".
The cooling water should flow through the cooling pipe to the electrode and return via annulus between the outside of the pipe and the

cooling holes.

APPENDIX (Clause3.1)

A-l. A-l.1 a) bj

A

MATERIAL FOR SPOT-WELDING ELECTRODES

INTRODUCTION
Spot-Welding electrodes perform four functions, namely: the They conduct the welding current current density in the weld zone; to the work and determine

They transmit the force to the area and determine the weld zone;

the pressure in surface

c) They dissipate the hrat from the weld zone, thus preventing fusion of the work; and d) They maintain alignment of the work.

A-1.2 Spot-welding electrodes carry currents ranging from 800 to 11 000 A/cm2. Since the quantity of heat developed is directly proportional to the square of the current, the time of current flow and the resistance of the path, it is obvious that the electrode materials should have a relatively high electrical conductivity to prevent electrodes from overheating. Also, the thermal conductivity should be sufficiently high to permit the heat generated at the work aild electrode faces to he dissipated readily, thus preventing the surfaces from fusing. A-1.3 The pressures on the electrodes mav range from 7 to 42 kgf/mm*. In addition, there may he considerable impact when the electrodes are brought together on the work. The&fore, in order to minimize deformation of the electrode face, the electrode should be of a material having high mechanical properties, particularly- at elevated temperatures. A-I.4 Thus, materials for spnt-welding electrodes should possess high electrical and thermal conductivity and high resistance to compressive In general, higher the conductivity of an electrode material deformation. the lower is its strength. The best electrode to use for a given application is one which possesses conductivity sulIicient to prevent overheating, but with the highest possible strength. A-2. RECOMMENDED MATERIAL

A-2.1 Copper is the basis of all spot-welding electrodes because of its high electrical and thermal conductivities. High conductivity hard-drawn copper has a conductivity of over 90 percent of International Annealed Copper Standard ( IACS) and is nsed in the welding of materials of high electrical conductivity, such as aluminium and its alloys. 30

IS : 4972 - 1968 A-2.2 The addition of a small percentage (0.5 to 1.0) of cadmium increases without much loss of conductivity the softening temperature of the alloy \\Fhich is greater than that could be obtained with pure copper. Such alloys, with a conductivity of over 85 percent IACS are used for Tellurium electrodes for welding tinplate and other coated material. copper, containing about 0.5 percent tellurium is also a high conductivity material ( 90 percent IACS) used for making electrodes for the spot-welding of aluminium and its alloys. A-2.3 Chromium copper containing about 0.5 to 0.8 percent of chromium ma!' be hardened by heat-treatment and cold working and is one of the hardest and strongest high conductivity copper alloys (85 percent IACS j; it is more resistant to wear and to softening at elevated temperatures than any materi:rls of equivalent conductivity and is one of the most generally used material for spot-welding electrodes. A-2.4 The addition of small quantities of cobalt and beryllium to copper provides an alloy with moderate conductivity and very high (higher than It is particularly suitable for chromium copper ) hardness and strength. welding materials of high strength at elevated temperatures, such as stainless steel and the heat-resisting alloys used for jet engines.
